sth_clerk.text: Jersey law is a mix of old Norman custom and its own statutes. The Bailiff presides, and twelve elected Jurats sit beside the judge. It's not like anywhere else in the British Isles.

Here's my favourite. If someone wrongs you, you can kneel and cry 'Haro! Haro! Haro! À l'aide, mon Prince, on me fait tort!' That's 'Help, my Prince, I am being wronged!' It's the Clameur de Haro. It stops them in their tracks until the court has heard the case.

then.text: Haro, haro, haro. Only joking. Don't cry haro unless you mean it.

else.text: {greeting} An advocate of the Royal Court. Jersey's version of a barrister, with better views.
Jersey isn't in the UK, and it was never in the EU. It's a Crown Dependency, like Guernsey and the Isle of Man.
We make our own laws in the States Assembly and set our own taxes. The UK looks after defence and foreign relations. We send no MPs to Westminster.
The King is our head of state. At dinners here he's toasted as Duke of Normandy. On Man he's Lord of Mann. He does collect titles.
Guernsey has its States of Deliberation, with Alderney and Sark in its Bailiwick, and Man has Tynwald, which says it's the oldest continuous parliament in the world.
Oh, and Man let some women vote in 1881, decades before Westminster did. They do mention it.
Noted in the Gazetteer, under How these isles work.
